source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 13 (PDF 4-17, printed 1-14); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 13 (Thermal Physics), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Thermal physics deals with the relationship between:

options.text: heat, work, temperature and other forms of energy

blocks.explanation: Thermal physics deals with the relationship between heat, work, temperature and other forms of energy (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: deals with the relationship between heat, work, temperature, and other forms of energy

blocks.prompt: 2 A large system containing many atoms or molecules is called a:
blocks.explanation: A system with many atoms or molecules is a macroscopic system (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: A large system containing many atoms or molecules is called a macroscopic system

blocks.prompt: 3 A system consisting of a single atom or molecule is called a:
blocks.explanation: A single atom or molecule forms a microscopic system (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: a system consisting of a single atom or molecule is called a microscopic system

blocks.prompt: 4 Which pair consists of properties of a macroscopic system?

options.text: Kinetic energy and momentum of one molecule
Charge and spin of one electron
Mass and speed of one atom

blocks.explanation: Temperature and pressure are thermal properties of the whole (macroscopic) system (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Macroscopic systems have properties such as temperature and pressure

blocks.prompt: 5 Kinetic energy and momentum are properties of a:
blocks.explanation: Microscopic systems (single atoms or molecules) have properties such as kinetic energy and momentum (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Microscopic systems have properties such as kinetic energy and momentum

blocks.prompt: 6 In thermal physics, the number of particles dealt with is of the order of:
blocks.explanation: Thermal physics deals with a large number of particles, of the order of Avogadro's number (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: we deal with large number of particles of the order of Avogadro's number

blocks.prompt: 7 The ideas of thermal physics can be extended to:

options.text: electron motion in metals and neutrons in neutron stars

blocks.explanation: The chapter says thermal physics can be extended to electron motion in metals and neutrons in neutron stars (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: We can extend it to the electron motion in metals and neutrons in neutron stars.

blocks.prompt: 8 Which of the following is listed as an application of the kinetic theory of gases in daily life?
blocks.explanation: Automobile engines, turbines, pumps, air conditioners and food production are listed applications (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: automobile engines, turbines, pumps, air conditioners

blocks.prompt: 9 To study thermal physics, knowledge of which two areas is needed?

options.text: Statistical mechanics and kinetic theory of gases

blocks.explanation: Thermal physics includes statistical mechanics and the kinetic theory of gases (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: includes the knowledge of statistical mechanics, and kinetic theory of gases

blocks.prompt: 10 Brownian motion is the:

options.text: random motion of small particles suspended in a fluid, caused by collisions with the fluid's molecules
uniform motion of a fluid in a pipe
motion of a body falling freely under gravity
steady flow of heat through a metal rod

blocks.explanation: Brownian motion is the random motion of small particles suspended in a fluid, caused by molecular collisions (13.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Brownian motion is the random motion of small particles suspended in a fluid

blocks.prompt: 11 Robert Brown, who first observed the random motion of pollen particles, was a:
blocks.explanation: Robert Brown was a botanist who observed the pollen particles under a microscope (13.1).

book_ref.quote: Robert Brown, a botanist observed under microscope

blocks.prompt: 12 In which year did Robert Brown make his observation of pollen particles moving randomly in a liquid?
blocks.explanation: Brown's observation was made in 1827 (13.1, book correction; the book prints 1927). 1905, 1908 and 1926 are Einstein, Perrin and Perrin's Nobel Prize.

book_ref.quote: Robert Brown made his observation in 1827

blocks.prompt: 13 When gas molecules collide with each other, the collision transfers or exchanges:
blocks.explanation: Collisions transfer or exchange momentum and energy between molecules (13.1).

book_ref.quote: collision transfers or exchanges the momentum and energy between the molecules

blocks.prompt: 14 A molecule that keeps on colliding with other molecules follows a:
blocks.explanation: Repeated collisions make the molecule follow a random or zig-zag motion (13.1, Fig. 13.1).

book_ref.quote: the colliding molecule follows a random or zig-zag motion

blocks.prompt: 15 In Brownian motion, which particles obtain greater speeds from collisions?
blocks.explanation: Lighter (smaller) particles obtain greater speeds from collisions (13.1).

book_ref.quote: Lighter particles obtain greater speeds from collisions

blocks.prompt: 16 Brownian movement is faster in a fluid of:

options.text: high density but no molecular motion

blocks.explanation: The speed of the particles is inversely proportional to viscosity; low viscosity gives faster Brownian movement (13.1).

book_ref.quote: Low viscosity of the fluid results in the faster Brownian movement.

blocks.prompt: 17 Viscosity describes the magnitude of the:
blocks.explanation: Viscosity is the magnitude of internal friction in a fluid, its resistance to flow (13.1).

book_ref.quote: Viscosity describes the magnitude of the internal friction in a fluid.

blocks.prompt: 18 Who explained the movement of pollen in a liquid in 1905?
blocks.explanation: Einstein explained the pollen movement in 1905; Perrin verified it experimentally in 1908 (13.1).

book_ref.quote: Albert Einstein explained the pollen movement in a liquid

blocks.prompt: 19 J Perrin, who experimentally verified Einstein's explanation of Brownian motion, received the Nobel Prize in physics in:
blocks.explanation: Perrin verified Einstein's explanation in 1908, which earned him the 1926 Nobel Prize in physics (13.1).

book_ref.quote: In 1908, a French physicist J Perrin experimentally verified

blocks.prompt: 20 Brownian motion represents one of the simple models of:
blocks.explanation: Brownian motion describes randomness and chaos, so it is a simple model of randomness (13.1).

book_ref.quote: it represents one of the simple models of randomness

blocks.prompt: 21 According to the kinetic theory, gas pressure arises due to:

options.text: attraction between gas particles at a distance
particles remaining at rest on the walls
particles colliding with each other and the walls of the container

blocks.explanation: Gas pressure arises from particles colliding with each other and with the container walls (13.2).

book_ref.quote: the gas pressure arises due to particles colliding with each other and the walls of the container

blocks.prompt: 22 Which of these is a transport property described by the kinetic theory of gases?
blocks.explanation: Viscosity, thermal conductivity and diffusivity are the transport properties named (13.2).

book_ref.quote: transport properties such as viscosity and thermal conductivity and diffusivity

blocks.prompt: 23 The kinetic molecular theory, as given in the chapter, applies to:

options.text: real gases at very high pressure only

blocks.explanation: The kinetic molecular theory applies to ideal gases (13.2).

book_ref.quote: The kinetic molecular theory applies to the ideal gases

blocks.prompt: 24 In the kinetic theory, gas particles are assumed to be:

options.text: tiny spheres far apart from one another compared to their sizes

blocks.explanation: Gases consist of a very large number of tiny spherical particles far apart compared to their sizes (13.2).

book_ref.quote: far apart from one another compared to their sizes

blocks.prompt: 25 The motion of gas particles according to the kinetic theory is:

options.text: slow and only along one axis
constant, rapid and in random directions
absent until the gas is heated

blocks.explanation: Gas particles are in constant rapid motion in random directions (13.2).

book_ref.quote: Gas particles are in constant rapid motion in random directions.

blocks.prompt: 26 Collisions between gas particles and the container walls are assumed to be:

options.text: sticky, so particles stay on the wall

blocks.explanation: In the kinetic theory these collisions are perfectly elastic, so no kinetic energy is lost (13.2).

book_ref.quote: Collisions between gas particles and the container walls are perfectly elastic collisions.

blocks.prompt: 27 Between collisions, the forces between gas particles of an ideal gas are:
blocks.explanation: There are no forces of attraction or repulsion between gas particles until they collide (13.2).

book_ref.quote: There are no forces of attraction or repulsion between gas particles

blocks.prompt: 28 The average kinetic energy of gas particles depends upon the gas's:
blocks.explanation: The average kinetic energy of gas particles depends on the temperature of the gas (13.2).

book_ref.quote: The average kinetic energy of gas particles is dependent upon the temperature of the gas.

blocks.prompt: 29 The mean free path is the average distance a moving particle covers:

options.text: before it undergoes a collision that significantly alters its direction or energy
between two walls of the container

blocks.explanation: Mean free path: the average distance a moving particle covers before a collision that significantly alters its direction or energy (13.2).

book_ref.quote: The mean free path is average distance a moving particle covered

blocks.prompt: 30 Compared with the volume of the empty spaces in a gas, the volume of the gas particles themselves is:
blocks.explanation: The volume of the gas particles is negligible compared to the empty spaces (13.2, Do you know?).

book_ref.quote: Volume of the gas particles is negligible compared to the volume of the empty spaces.

blocks.text: 13.3 Pressure in a Gas and Derivation of PV = ⅓Nm<v²>

blocks.prompt: 31 The kinetic-theory equation for gas pressure relates pressure and volume to which microscopic properties of the molecules?
blocks.explanation: The equation relates the macroscopic P and V to the microscopic mass and speed of the molecules (13.3).

book_ref.quote: relates the macroscopic properties of a gas (pressure and volume) to the microscopic properties of its molecules (mass and speed)

blocks.prompt: 32 The pressure of a gas is the:

options.text: total kinetic energy of all molecules
mass of gas per unit volume
force exerted per unit area of the container walls by molecular collisions

blocks.explanation: Pressure is the force per unit area on the walls due to molecular collisions (13.3).

book_ref.quote: The pressure of a gas is defined as the force exerted per unit area of the container walls

blocks.prompt: 33 When the temperature of a gas in a fixed container is increased, its pressure:

options.text: increases because molecules move faster and collide more
stays the same because volume is fixed

blocks.explanation: Higher temperature increases molecular speed, giving more collisions and higher pressure (13.3).

book_ref.quote: leading to more collisions, and consequently, a higher pressure

blocks.prompt: 34 The general gas constant R is related to the Boltzmann constant k_B and Avogadro's number N_A by:
blocks.explanation: R equals N_A k_B, so PV = nRT becomes PV = nN_Ak_BT (13.3).

book_ref.quote: R is general gas constant equals to N_A k_B

blocks.prompt: 35 The value and unit of the Boltzmann constant are:

book_ref.quote: k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ is the Boltzmann constant

blocks.prompt: 36 Using n = N/N_A, the gas law PV = nRT can be written as:
blocks.explanation: PV = nN_Ak_BT and n = N/N_A give PV = Nk_BT, Eq. (13.2).

book_ref.quote: The number of moles in terms of number of particle N is defined as

blocks.prompt: 37 How many molecules are in 1.0 m³ of an ideal gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 300 K? (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: The ideal gas obeys the gas law which would relate the gas temperature with other parameters

blocks.prompt: 38 A molecule of mass m moving with velocity vₓ strikes a wall elastically and rebounds. The change in its momentum is:
blocks.explanation: Δp = −mvₓ − (mvₓ) = −2mvₓ (13.3).

book_ref.quote: its momentum changes from mv to -mv

blocks.prompt: 39 A gas molecule of mass 5.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg moving at 500 m s⁻¹ along the x-axis rebounds elastically from a wall. The magnitude of its change in momentum is:

book_ref.quote: Consider a collision in which the molecule with velocity v strikes one face of the cube along x-axis.

blocks.prompt: 40 In a cube of side L, the distance a molecule travels between two consecutive collisions with the same wall is:
blocks.explanation: It goes to the opposite wall and back, a distance 2L, so the time is 2L/vₓ, Eq. (13.3).

book_ref.quote: The molecule travels a distance 2L between the consecutive collisions

blocks.prompt: 41 A molecule moves with vₓ = 400 m s⁻¹ in a cubical box of side 0.20 m. The time between its consecutive collisions with the same wall is:

book_ref.quote: Hence, time between two consecutive collisions with one side of the cube is:

blocks.prompt: 42 The average force exerted on a wall by one molecule of mass m moving with x-velocity vₓ in a cube of side L is:
blocks.explanation: F = |Δp|/Δt = 2mvₓ/(2L/vₓ) = mvₓ²/L, Eq. (13.4).

book_ref.quote: This expression represents the force exerted on the container wall by one molecule in the x-direction.

blocks.prompt: 43 A molecule of mass 5.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg moves with vₓ = 400 m s⁻¹ in a cubical box of side 0.10 m. The average force it exerts on one wall is:

book_ref.quote: The average force exerted by the wall of cube on the molecule can be found using Newton's second law of motion.

blocks.prompt: 44 The pressure exerted on a wall by one molecule in a cube of volume V = L³ is:
blocks.explanation: P = F/L² = (mvₓ²/L)/L² = mvₓ²/L³ = mvₓ²/V, Eq. (13.5).

book_ref.quote: This is the pressure exerted on container wall by one molecule.

blocks.prompt: 45 If a container holds N particles each of mass m, the total mass M of the gas is:
blocks.explanation: Total mass is the number of particles times the mass of a particle, M = mN (13.3).

book_ref.quote: then total mass is the number of particles times mass of the particle

blocks.prompt: 46 The velocities are squared before averaging in the kinetic theory because:

options.text: the simple average of vₓ and −vₓ is zero
the mass of a molecule is negative

blocks.explanation: A molecule strikes with vₓ and leaves with −vₓ, so the simple average is zero; squaring avoids this (13.3).

book_ref.quote: which would result in average velocity zero

blocks.prompt: 47 The root mean square (rms) velocity is:

options.text: the average of the square roots of the velocities
the square root of the average of the squares of the velocities
the square of the average velocity
the sum of all velocities divided by two

blocks.explanation: rms velocity = √<v²>, the square root of the mean of the squares (13.3; Eq. 13.8 book correction).

book_ref.quote: it is known as the root mean square (rms) velocity

blocks.prompt: 48 Four molecules have speeds 1, 2, 3 and 4 m s⁻¹. Their rms speed is:
blocks.explanation: <v²> = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16)/4 = 7.5 m² s⁻²; vᵣₘₛ = √7.5 = 2.7 m s⁻¹ (the mean speed is 2.5 m s⁻¹) (13.3).

book_ref.quote: If we take the square root of the average square of the velocities

blocks.prompt: 49 For molecules moving randomly with the same average speed in all three directions, <v²> is equal to:

book_ref.quote: have the same average speed in all three directions

blocks.prompt: 50 For a gas, <v²> = 2.7 × 10⁵ m² s⁻². The value of <vₓ²> is:

book_ref.quote: Since the molecules are moving randomly in all directions

blocks.prompt: 51 The kinetic-theory expression for an ideal gas of N molecules each of mass m in volume V is:
blocks.explanation: PV = ⅓Nm<v²>, Eq. (13.13).

book_ref.quote: This is the pressure of the gas molecules on the wall.

blocks.prompt: 52 In terms of density ρ, the pressure of a gas is:
blocks.explanation: Since ρ = mN/V, P = ⅓ρ<v²> (13.3; the printed PV = ⅓ρ<v²> is a misprint, see the book correction).

book_ref.quote: This is the pressure of the gas which depends on the density and root mean square of velocity.

blocks.prompt: 53 An ideal gas has a density of 2.0 kg m⁻³ at a pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa. The rms speed of its molecules is:

book_ref.quote: Pressure is defined as; P = ⅓ρ<v²>

blocks.prompt: 54 A gas of density 1.2 kg m⁻³ has an rms molecular speed of 500 m s⁻¹. Its pressure is:

book_ref.quote: To find the rms value, take the square root of the mean-square-speed

blocks.prompt: 55 If the rms speed of the molecules of a gas is doubled while its density stays the same, its pressure becomes:
blocks.explanation: P = ⅓ρvᵣₘₛ², so doubling vᵣₘₛ makes P four times (13.3).

blocks.prompt: 56 In P = ⅔N₀<K.E._T>, the symbol N₀ stands for:

options.text: the total mass of the gas
N/V, the number of molecules per unit volume

blocks.explanation: From P = (2/3)(N/V)<½mv²> with N/V = N₀, P = ⅔N₀<K.E._T> (13.3).

book_ref.quote: Rearranging the pressure, Eq. (13.13) for P, and substituting the density

blocks.prompt: 57 A gas has 2.5 × 10²⁵ molecules per m³, each with average translational kinetic energy 6.0 × 10⁻²¹ J. The gas pressure is:

book_ref.quote: The pressure in terms of density can be written as:

blocks.prompt: 58 The mass of one molecule of a gas of molecular mass 40 u is: (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)
59 Taking the mass of a nitrogen molecule as 4.6 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, its rms speed at 400 K is: (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: Mass of Nitrogen N₂ = 28 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 4.6 × 10⁻²⁶ kg

blocks.prompt: 60 Compared with the speed of sound in air (about 340 m s⁻¹), the rms speed of air molecules at room temperature is:
blocks.explanation: The rms speeds (about 481 m s⁻¹ for O₂ and 515 m s⁻¹ for N₂) are much greater than the speed of sound (13.3).

book_ref.quote: The speed of air molecules is much greater than the speed of sound

blocks.prompt: 61 When a popcorn kernel is heated, the moisture trapped inside it:

options.text: becomes steam and raises the pressure inside
escapes slowly without any pressure change

blocks.explanation: The trapped moisture becomes steam; the pressure in the kernel rises and ruptures the cover (Daily life examples).

book_ref.quote: the moisture trapped in popcorn kernel becomes steam

blocks.prompt: 62 When the pressure in a popcorn kernel ruptures its cover, it releases:
blocks.explanation: The rupture releases the gelatinous starch, which becomes solid after cooling (Daily life examples).

book_ref.quote: it ruptures the corn cover releasing the gelatinous starch

blocks.prompt: 63 Pumping air into a car tyre raises the pressure inside it because:

options.text: more molecules in a limited volume collide more frequently with the walls

blocks.explanation: More air molecules in a limited volume give more frequent collisions with the tyre walls, raising the pressure (Daily life examples).

book_ref.quote: the number of air molecules increases which raises the air pressure inside the tyres

blocks.prompt: 64 What gives a car tyre its hardness so that it bears the car's weight?

options.text: The temperature of the road only

blocks.explanation: The pressure of the air gives the tyre its hardness and lets it bear the car's weight (Daily life examples).

book_ref.quote: The pressure gives the tyre its hardness

blocks.text: 13.4 Average Translational Kinetic Energy of a Gas

blocks.prompt: 65 The Boltzmann constant is equal to:

book_ref.quote: The gas constant R is related with Boltzmann constant and Avogadro number.

blocks.prompt: 66 The rms speed of the molecules of an ideal gas at absolute temperature T is:

book_ref.quote: where N/n = N_A is the number of molecules in one mole and it is Avogadro number.

blocks.prompt: 67 The molar mass mN_A of oxygen is 0.032 kg mol⁻¹. Its rms speed at 300 K is: (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: Equating these equations, we have

blocks.prompt: 68 If the absolute temperature of a gas is made four times, the rms speed of its molecules becomes:
blocks.explanation: vᵣₘₛ ∝ √T, so 4T gives √4 = 2 times the rms speed (13.4).

book_ref.quote: is the average translational kinetic energy and it is denoted by

blocks.prompt: 69 The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at absolute temperature T is:
blocks.explanation: <K.E._T> = (3/2)k_BT, so temperature is a direct measure of the average translational K.E. (13.4).

book_ref.quote: the temperature of a gas is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules

blocks.prompt: 70 The average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 400 K is: (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: The average translational kinetic energy of the molecules in a gas is given by a simple constant times the temperature.

blocks.prompt: 71 At what temperature is the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule 1.035 × 10⁻²⁰ J? (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: Substituting v²ᵣₘₛ value in Eq. (13.17)

blocks.prompt: 72 If the absolute temperature of a gas is doubled, the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules:
blocks.explanation: <K.E.> = (3/2)k_BT is directly proportional to T, so it doubles (13.4).

book_ref.quote: So, if this model is accurate

blocks.prompt: 73 The value of k_BT at 200 K is: (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: For an air molecule at room temperature (300 K), the quantity k_BT is

blocks.prompt: 74 Energies like k_BT of a single molecule are often expressed in electron volts because:

options.text: the joule is not an energy unit
they are very small in joules
they are very large in joules

blocks.explanation: k_BT is a very small quantity in joules (about 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ J at 300 K), so the electron volt is used (13.4).

book_ref.quote: For such a small quantity, we use electron volt instead of joule (J).

blocks.prompt: 75 One electron volt is the kinetic energy gained by:

options.text: an electron accelerated through a potential difference of one volt
a proton moving at 1 m s⁻¹
one mole of electrons at 1 K
an electron at rest in a field of 1 V m⁻¹

blocks.explanation: The electron volt is the K.E. of an electron accelerated through a voltage difference of one volt (13.4).

book_ref.quote: The electron volt is the kinetic energy of an electron that has been accelerated through a voltage difference of one volt

blocks.prompt: 76 An energy of 0.050 eV is equal to: (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)

book_ref.quote: accelerated through a voltage difference of one volt: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

blocks.prompt: 77 Using k_B = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV K⁻¹, the value of k_BT at 500 K is:

book_ref.quote: Boltzmann constant is 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV K⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 78 Knowledge from kinetic theory about pollutants and the atmosphere is used to develop systems that:
blocks.explanation: Kinetic theory helps understand pollutant-atmosphere interaction, used to develop air-quality monitoring systems (13.4).

book_ref.quote: Kinetic theory helps to understand the interaction between pollutants and the atmosphere.

blocks.prompt: 79 Statistical physics is the branch of physics that uses:
blocks.explanation: For a large number of molecules we use statistical physics, which uses probability theory (13.5).

book_ref.quote: It is the branch of physics that uses probability theory.

blocks.prompt: 80 Atoms and molecules of a system may exist in different energy states E₁, E₂, E₃, ... because of their different:
blocks.explanation: Atoms and molecules exist in different energy states due to different speeds (13.5).

book_ref.quote: may exist in different energy states (levels)

blocks.prompt: 81 Who, in 1860, derived an expression for the distribution of molecular speeds in a system at thermal equilibrium?
blocks.explanation: James Clerk Maxwell derived the speed-distribution expression in 1860 (13.5; the book misspells his name).

book_ref.quote: derived an expression that describes the distribution of molecular speeds

blocks.prompt: 82 Maxwell's predictions about the distribution of molecular speeds were confirmed by experiment about:
blocks.explanation: Experiments confirmed Maxwell's predictions about 60 years later (13.5).

book_ref.quote: About 60 years later, experiments were performed to confirm Maxwell's predictions.

blocks.prompt: 83 The Boltzmann kinetic equation describes:

options.text: the focal length of a lens
the motion of a single planet
the dynamic processes in gases having a large number of molecules

blocks.explanation: The Boltzmann kinetic equation describes dynamic processes in gases with a large number of molecules (13.5).

book_ref.quote: This equation describes the dynamic processes in gases having large number of molecules.

blocks.prompt: 84 According to the Boltzmann distribution law, the ratio of the populations of a higher and a lower energy state is:
blocks.explanation: N₂/N₁ = e^(−ΔE/k_BT), Eq. (13.19); e^(−ΔE/k_BT) is the Boltzmann factor (13.5).

book_ref.quote: N₁ and N₂ are the population of lower and higher energy states

blocks.prompt: 85 Two energy levels differ by ΔE = k_BT. The ratio N₂/N₁ of the populations of the higher and lower levels is about:

book_ref.quote: ΔE = (E₂ – E₁) is the energy difference between these states

blocks.prompt: 86 If the energy difference between two levels is ΔE = 2k_BT, the ratio N₂/N₁ is about:

book_ref.quote: This equation is known as the Boltzmann distribution law

blocks.prompt: 87 According to the Boltzmann distribution law, at a given temperature:

options.text: more particles are in lower energy states than in higher ones
more particles are in higher energy states
the lowest state is always empty

blocks.explanation: Because N₂/N₁ = e^(−ΔE/k_BT) < 1, more particles reside in lower energy states (13.5).

book_ref.quote: more particles reside in lower energy states than in higher ones

blocks.prompt: 88 The probability of finding molecules in a particular energy state varies with the energy E as:

options.text: it does not depend on E

blocks.explanation: The probability varies exponentially as the negative of energy divided by k_BT (13.5).

book_ref.quote: varies exponentially as the negative of the energy divided by k_BT

blocks.prompt: 89 In a gas container, a molecule undergoes about how many collisions every second?
blocks.explanation: A molecule undergoes billions of collisions every second, each changing its speed and K.E. (13.5).

book_ref.quote: a molecule undergoes billions of collisions every second

blocks.prompt: 90 The Boltzmann constant k_B can be described as:
blocks.explanation: In E_av = (3/2)k_BT, k_B is effectively the gas constant per molecule (13.5).

book_ref.quote: is effectively the gas constant per molecule

blocks.prompt: 91 At a fixed temperature, the number density of gas molecules is:

options.text: proportional to the square of the pressure

blocks.explanation: The number density is directly proportional to the pressure (13.5); from P = (N/V)k_BT.

book_ref.quote: The number density is directly proportional to the pressure.

blocks.prompt: 92 Neutron stars are among the densest known objects in the universe, second only to:
blocks.explanation: Neutron stars are second only to black holes in density (Neutron stars).

book_ref.quote: Neutron stars are among the densest known objects in the universe, second only to black holes.

blocks.prompt: 93 Because of their extremely high density, matter inside neutron stars behaves like a:
blocks.explanation: Matter inside neutron stars behaves like a degenerate gas (Neutron stars).

book_ref.quote: matter inside neutron stars behaves like a degenerate gas

blocks.prompt: 94 Young neutron stars that rotate rapidly and emit beams of radiation are called:
blocks.explanation: Rapidly rotating young neutron stars emitting beams of radiation are pulsars (Neutron stars).

book_ref.quote: These are known as pulsars.

blocks.prompt: 95 Pulsar radiation is believed to be produced when:

options.text: strong magnetic fields channel matter toward the magnetic poles of neutron stars
hydrogen is fused into helium on the surface
light is reflected from nearby planets

blocks.explanation: Scientists believe pulsar radiation is produced when strong magnetic fields channel matter to the magnetic poles (Neutron stars).

book_ref.quote: strong magnetic fields channel matter toward the magnetic poles

blocks.prompt: 96 When a star collapses to form a neutron star, its magnetic field:

options.text: is greatly intensified as field lines are squeezed closer

blocks.explanation: During collapse the field lines are squeezed together, so the magnetic field is greatly intensified (Neutron stars).

book_ref.quote: its magnetic field is also greatly intensified

blocks.prompt: 97 According to NASA estimates, the number of neutron stars in the Milky Way may be up to:
blocks.explanation: There may be up to a billion neutron stars in the Milky Way (Neutron stars).

book_ref.quote: there may be up to a billion neutron stars in the Milky Way galaxy

blocks.prompt: 98 The Sun was formed about:
blocks.explanation: The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a solar nebula (Our star).

book_ref.quote: It was formed about 4.6 billion years ago

blocks.prompt: 99 The huge cloud of gas and dust from which the Sun formed is called a:
blocks.explanation: The Sun formed from a huge cloud of gas and dust called a solar nebula (Our star).

book_ref.quote: a huge cloud of gas and dust called a solar nebula

blocks.prompt: 100 A protostar forms when:

options.text: the star explodes as a supernova
gravitational contraction raises the temperature at the centre of the gas cloud

blocks.explanation: Gravitational contraction increased the central temperature and a protostar was formed (Our star).

book_ref.quote: Due to gravitational contraction, the temperature at the centre increased and a protostar was formed.

blocks.prompt: 101 In the Sun's core, nuclear fusion changes:
blocks.explanation: Nuclear fusion in the hot core changes hydrogen into helium, releasing a large amount of energy (Our star).

book_ref.quote: nuclear fusion started in which hydrogen changed into helium

blocks.prompt: 102 At present the Sun is in which stage of its life?
blocks.explanation: The Sun is now in the main sequence stage, converting hydrogen into helium (Our star).

book_ref.quote: At present, the Sun is in the main sequence stage

blocks.prompt: 103 Which is the correct order of the later life stages of the Sun?

options.text: Main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
Main sequence → white dwarf → red giant → planetary nebula
Red giant → main sequence → white dwarf → planetary nebula
Main sequence → planetary nebula → red giant → white dwarf

blocks.explanation: The Sun's stages: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, planetary nebula, white dwarf (Our star).

book_ref.quote: The life stages of the Sun are: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, planetary nebula, and white dwarf.

blocks.prompt: 104 The Sun transfers its heat energy to the Earth mainly by:
blocks.explanation: The Sun transfers its energy mainly by radiation (Our star).

book_ref.quote: transfers this energy mainly by radiation

blocks.prompt: 105 A star has mass 3 × 10³⁰ kg and radius 6 × 10⁸ m. Using P_g ≈ GM²/R⁴ (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²), its gravitational pressure is about:

book_ref.quote: Calculate gravitational pressure and compare it with internal pressure

blocks.prompt: 106 A star's gravitational pressure is 2.7 × 10¹⁴ Pa and its internal pressure is 5 × 10¹⁴ Pa. The star will:

options.text: expand and may evolve into a red giant

blocks.explanation: Internal pressure is larger than gravitational pressure, so the star expands and may become a red giant (Our star, Example 13.5).

book_ref.quote: Internal pressure dominates, therefore, the star will expand and may evolve into a red giant.

blocks.prompt: 107 If the gravitational pressure of a star is much larger than its internal pressure, the star will:

options.text: contract and may collapse into a neutron star or black hole
turn into a nebula at once

blocks.explanation: Gravity is stronger, so the star contracts and may eventually collapse, possibly forming a neutron star or black hole (Our star, Example 13.4).

book_ref.quote: Gravity is stronger, therefore, the star will contract and may eventually collapse

blocks.prompt: 108 One teaspoon of neutron-star material would have a mass of over:
blocks.explanation: A teaspoon of neutron-star material would have a mass over 5.5 × 10¹² kg, about 900 times the Great Pyramid (For your information).

book_ref.quote: one teaspoon of its material would have a mass over 5.5 × 10¹² kg

blocks.prompt: 109 At neutron-star density, the entire mass of the Earth would fit into a sphere of diameter about:
blocks.explanation: The whole Earth's mass at neutron-star density would fit in a sphere 305 m in diameter (For your information).

book_ref.quote: would fit into a sphere 305 m in diameter

blocks.prompt: 110 When the kinetic theory of gases is extended to stars and galaxies, it helps us understand:

options.text: the evolution of stars and gas atoms in a stellar atmosphere
the refraction of light in glass

blocks.explanation: Extended to astrophysical systems, kinetic theory helps understand stellar evolution and gas atoms in stellar atmospheres (13.6).

book_ref.quote: helps us understand the evolution of stars in a galaxy

blocks.prompt: 111 The lifetimes of stars range from:

options.text: a few days to a few years
exactly 4.6 billion years for every star
a few seconds to a few hours
a few million years to trillions of years

blocks.explanation: Stars can live from a few million years to trillions of years (13.6).

book_ref.quote: Star can have range of lifetime from a few million years to trillions of years.

blocks.prompt: 112 Which stars have the longest lifetimes?

options.text: Stars ten times the Sun's mass

blocks.explanation: The least massive stars, red dwarfs, live longest; the most massive live only a few million years (13.6, book correction).

book_ref.quote: It is the least massive stars (red dwarfs) that live longest

blocks.prompt: 113 All stars are formed from clouds of gas and dust which are often called:
blocks.explanation: Stars form from clouds of gas and dust called nebulae or molecular clouds (13.6).

book_ref.quote: which are often called nebulae or molecular clouds

blocks.prompt: 114 As a cloud of gas and dust contracts to form a star, its:
blocks.explanation: As the cloud contracts, its density and temperature rise because the K.E. of particles rises (K.E. ∝ T) (13.6).

book_ref.quote: As the cloud contracts, its density and temperature increase

blocks.prompt: 115 A star is stable when:

options.text: the inward gravitational force is exactly balanced by the outward pressure
gravity is much greater than pressure

blocks.explanation: A stable star forms when inward gravity is exactly balanced by outward pressure (13.6).

book_ref.quote: A stable star is formed when the inward gravitational force is exactly balanced by the outward pressure.

blocks.prompt: 116 In the hydrostatic equation ΔP/Δr = −GMᵣρᵣ/r², the negative sign shows that:

options.text: pressure decreases outward from the centre

blocks.explanation: The negative sign shows that pressure decreases outward while gravity pulls inward (13.6).

book_ref.quote: negative sign indicates that pressure decreases outward

blocks.prompt: 117 In the hydrostatic equation of a star, Mᵣ stands for:

options.text: the total mass of the galaxy
the mass of one hydrogen atom
the mass enclosed within radius r

blocks.explanation: Mᵣ is the mass enclosed within radius r; ρᵣ is the density at radius r (13.6).

book_ref.quote: M_r is mass enclosed within radius r

blocks.prompt: 118 As the core temperature of a star rises, nuclear fusion begins in which:

options.text: hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium

blocks.explanation: Fusion lets hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium, releasing immense energy that powers the star (13.6).

book_ref.quote: allowing hydrogen nuclei to combine and form helium

blocks.prompt: 119 In the red giant stage, stars with at least about half the Sun's mass fuse helium to produce:
blocks.explanation: Such stars can start helium fusion, producing heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen (13.6).

book_ref.quote: capable of initiating helium fusion in their cores

blocks.prompt: 120 In more massive stars, the fusion of heavier elements continues in successive stages up to:
blocks.explanation: In massive stars fusion continues, forming increasingly complex nuclei up to iron (13.6).

book_ref.quote: forming increasingly complex nuclei up to iron

blocks.prompt: 121 When a low or intermediate mass star exhausts its nuclear fuel, its core contracts into a:

options.text: white dwarf, while the outer layers form a planetary nebula

blocks.explanation: In low and intermediate mass stars the core becomes a dense white dwarf and the outer layers form a planetary nebula (13.6).

book_ref.quote: the core contracts into a dense white dwarf

blocks.prompt: 122 Stars with masses roughly ten times that of the Sun end their lives in a:

options.text: quiet change into a white dwarf only
supernova explosion, leaving a neutron star or black hole

blocks.explanation: Such stars undergo a supernova; the iron core collapses into a neutron star or black hole (13.6).

book_ref.quote: stars with masses roughly ten times greater than that of the Sun undergo a dramatic supernova explosion

blocks.prompt: 123 In the life cycle of a massive star, the stage that follows the red supergiant is a:
blocks.explanation: After the red supergiant comes a supernova (Fig. 13.5; the printed label 'Positron' is a misprint) (13.6).

book_ref.quote: This stage is a supernova, as drawn above.

blocks.prompt: 124 Why has no red dwarf yet completed its life cycle?

options.text: The universe is not yet old enough
Red dwarfs never use any fuel
Red dwarfs explode too early to be seen
Red dwarfs are hotter than all other stars

blocks.explanation: Red dwarfs evolve very slowly; the universe is not yet old enough for any to finish (13.6).

book_ref.quote: The universe is not yet old enough for any red dwarf to have completed its life cycle.

blocks.prompt: 125 After exhausting their hydrogen fuel, red dwarfs are expected to evolve into:
blocks.explanation: Theoretical models say red dwarfs become hotter and brighter, then evolve into low mass white dwarfs (13.6).

book_ref.quote: evolving into low mass white dwarfs

blocks.prompt: 126 The final fate of a star depends primarily on its:
blocks.explanation: The final fate of a star depends primarily on its mass (13.6).

book_ref.quote: The final fate of a star depends primarily on its mass.

blocks.prompt: 127 A star is 4.0 parsec away. Its distance in light years is about: (1 parsec ≈ 3.26 light years)
blocks.explanation: 4.0 × 3.26 = 13.04 ≈ 13 light years (13.6, Do you know?).

book_ref.quote: one parsec is approximately 3.26 light years
